name: William of Occam
school: Franciscan scholasticism (Augustinian/Platonist current, opposed to strict Thomism)
major_ideas: Occam's separation of logic from metaphysics and theology
Marsiglio's and Occam's theory of popular and conciliar sovereignty
biography: The chapter's central figure (ca. 1290-1349/50), pupil then rival of Duns Scotus; involved in the Franciscan poverty controversy against Pope John XXII, exiled to Munich under Emperor Louis's protection; developed Occam's razor, a nominalist logic sharply separated from metaphysics and theology, and (with Marsiglio) an influential political theory of popular and conciliar sovereignty preferred by Luther among the schoolmen.
central_doctrines: Occam's razor: The methodological principle, associated with (though not verbatim from) William of Occam, that explanations should not posit more entities than are necessary; often rendered 'Entities are not to be multiplied without necessity,' closer to Occam's actual formulation 'It is vain to do with more what can be done with fewer.' Occam's separation of logic from metaphysics and theology: Occam's methodological program, per the interpretation of Ernest Moody that Russell endorses, of restoring a purified Aristotelian logic as an independent instrument of natural philosophy, freed from the Augustinian and Arabic metaphysical/theological accretions that (via Porphyry's questions about genera and species) had entangled logic with metaphysics since late antiquity. Marsiglio's and Occam's theory of popular and conciliar sovereignty: The fourteenth-century political theory, developed chiefly by Marsiglio of Padua and adopted in modified form by Occam, that legislative and even ecclesiastical authority derives from the sovereignty of the people (including the laity), to be exercised through elected representative councils rather than through unilateral papal or imperial authority.
key_arguments: Occam's resolution of the flatus-vocis/universals fallacy

russell_view: Russell is notably deflationary about Roger Bacon's popular reputation, crediting his genuine value of experiment and his geographical influence on Columbus, but judging him 'not, to my mind, so scientific as is sometimes thought' and unsystematic despite his encyclopedic learning; he also flatly denies the popular claim that Bacon invented gunpowder. Russell treats Duns Scotus's metaphysics respectfully as a serious, more Platonic-leaning alternative to Aquinas on individuation, tracing its modern descendants carefully. His treatment of Occam is the chapter's most sympathetic: Russell explicitly follows Ernest Moody's revisionist interpretation over the common tendency to read Occam as a precursor of Descartes or Kant, praises Occam's razor as a principle Russell himself has found fruitful, and credits Occam's separation of logic from theology with encouraging scientific research. Russell's tone throughout combines historical caution (repeatedly correcting popular misattributions -- Occam's razor's exact wording, Bacon and gunpowder) with genuine philosophical engagement, particularly on individuation and Occam's logic.
why_this_matters: Franciscan philosophers (Bacon, Scotus, Occam) were generally less strictly Thomistic and retained more Augustinian/Platonist influence than Dominicans. Roger Bacon valued experiment and mathematics highly but was, per Russell, encyclopedic rather than systematic, and less purely 'scientific' than his later reputation suggests.
